practicalQuestion: How should high-minute, low-minute, and returning athletes receive different strength, speed, and conditioning exposures during a short turnaround between competitions?

decisionContext.population: Collegiate roster with different recent competition exposures
decisionContext.phase: Seventy-two to ninety-six hours between competitions
decisionContext.outcome: Preserve readiness while addressing underexposure and continued progression by subgroup
decisionContext.constraints: One full-team field session; limited weight-room access; returning athletes remain under medical and rehabilitation plans

evidenceConfidence.rationale: The pack has indirect evidence that match minutes create different running exposures and that the timing of near-maximal speed running within a turnaround is associated with match hamstring injuries. None of it tests subgroup-specific dosing in a 72 to 96 hour window. There is no evidence on strength or weight-room work, and evidence for returning athletes is expert opinion only. All of it comes from professional or elite players, not collegiate athletes.

dimensions.sourceReview: One relevant source (match minutes and weekly load) is full-text screened. The speed-exposure, return-to-play, and wellness sources are legacy records whose summaries were not full-text reviewed. Claims here rely only on quoted original text.
dimensions.directness: Indirect. One study describes load gaps by match minutes but only in six-day weeks. The speed-exposure study is observational and links timing of sprint exposure to injury, not to readiness or performance. No source tests strength exposure or a compensatory top-up.
dimensions.consistency: No material disagreement among the cited claims, but each addresses a different part of the question, so they cannot confirm one another.
dimensions.transferability: Low to moderate. Populations are professional soccer players, elite European soccer teams, and elite Australian football players. Sex is not reported in the cited excerpts, and no collegiate or non-football team sport data are included.

bottomLine.text: In professional soccer, players with more match time accumulated more weekly running load, so low-minute and non-playing athletes can carry an exposure gap. In elite soccer, near-maximal speed exposure was less common in short turnarounds, and no match hamstring injuries occurred when exposures above 95% of maximal sprinting speed fell two days before a match. This was an observational association. The library does not test how to dose each subgroup in a 72 to 96 hour window, says nothing about strength work, and offers only expert opinion for returning athletes.

actions.title: Low-minute and non-playing athletes: options for the exposure gap
actions.text: Players with less match time accumulated less weekly running load in the one study available. Options are to add supplementary running exposure for these athletes within the full-team session, or to accept the gap until a longer turnaround. The evidence comes from six-day weeks and does not test a top-up dose or show that top-ups improve outcomes.

actions.title: Near-maximal speed: options on timing
actions.text: In elite soccer, only a minority of three-day turnarounds included runs above 85% of maximal sprinting speed. No match hamstring injuries occurred when exposures above 95% fell two days before the match, and injuries still happened when players were not exposed at all. One option is a brief near-maximal speed exposure in the field session if it falls about two days out. The other is to omit it when timing or individual status makes it unsuitable. The design was observational, so this is not proof of protection.

actions.title: High-minute athletes: no tested dose
actions.text: High-minute players already carry more accumulated running load. The evidence does not test a specific reduced or maintenance dose for them in a short turnaround. Options are to keep them at lower volume within the shared session, or to include only short near-maximal speed exposure when staff judge them recovered. Either choice is professional judgment, not an evidence-based prescription.

actions.title: Returning athletes: stay inside the medical plan
actions.text: Experts in one elite football study felt that, judged by subsequent injury risk, players generally return too early. They cited more time for conditioning and psychological readiness as possible reasons. Any team-session or speed exposure for returning athletes should follow their existing medical and rehabilitation plans rather than the subgroup options above.

monitoring.label: Exposure since last competition
monitoring.text: Track each athlete's match minutes and running exposure since the last competition to identify who carries a gap. This follows the finding that more match time meant more accumulated load.

monitoring.label: Near-maximal speed log
monitoring.text: Record whether each athlete reached near-maximal speed during the turnaround and on which day. The injury association in elite soccer depended on both the speed threshold and the day of exposure.

monitoring.label: Wellness questionnaires
monitoring.text: In elite Australian football, prematch wellness did not relate to external match load. Wellness scores should not be the only input for setting subgroup exposure. This is professional caution, not a tested monitoring rule.

guardrails.text: For returning athletes, progression, exposure, and clearance decisions stay with the treating clinicians and the rehabilitation plan. This brief does not clear any athlete.
The timing finding on near-maximal speed is an observational association. Do not present it to athletes or coaches as proven injury prevention.
No source sets a subgroup dose for a 72 to 96 hour turnaround. Any dose chosen is staff judgment informed by, not derived from, this evidence.

limitations.text: All cited data come from professional soccer, elite European soccer, or elite Australian football. Sex is not reported in the cited excerpts, and no collegiate athletes were studied.
The match-minutes study analysed only weeks with six days between matches, which is longer than the 72 to 96 hour window in this question.
The cited claims cover running load and sprint exposure only. Nothing in the pack addresses strength or weight-room exposure by subgroup.
Guidance for returning athletes rests on expert opinion about return timing, not on data about team-session exposure during short turnarounds.

whatCouldChange.text: A study testing subgroup-specific running or strength top-ups for low-minute athletes in short turnarounds, with readiness or injury outcomes.
Collegiate or controlled data on when to place near-maximal speed exposure within a three- to four-day turnaround.

claims.text: In professional soccer players, those with more match playing time had higher accumulated weekly load for most variables, particularly total distance and high metabolic load distance, compared with players under 60 minutes or not playing.

evidence.excerpt: players (as a whole o per demarcation) with more match playing time had a higher accumulative weekly load for most of the variables, but particularly at TD and HMLD (90-min and >60-min vs. <60-min and 0-min)

claims.text: The match-minutes study compared in-season weekly load of professional soccer players by match time and analysed only training weeks with six days between matches.

evidence.excerpt: The aim of this study was to compare weekly accumulative load during the in-season competitive period by professional soccer players according to the amount of time played in official matches
Due to variations in the number of days between matches [12-14], the present study only analysed training weeks where players had six

claims.text: In elite soccer, near-maximal speed exposures were more common in longer turnarounds and at lower thresholds. For example, 18% of three-day turnarounds included runs above 85% of maximal sprinting speed, compared with 72% of seven-day turnarounds.

evidence.excerpt: The longer the length of the turnarounds and the lower the speed thresholds, the greater the number (and proportion) of near-to-MSS exposures (e.g., 18%, 45% and 72% of turnarounds with > 85% runs for 3, 5 and 7-turnarounds, respectively).

claims.text: In elite soccer, regardless of turnaround length, there were no match hamstring injuries when exposures above 95% of maximal sprinting speed occurred two days before the match, while injuries still happened when players were not exposed at all.

evidence.excerpt: Finally, irrespective of the turnaround length, there were no match hamstring injuries when > 95% MSS exposures occurred at D-2, while in contrast, injuries still happened when players were not exposed at all,

claims.text: The speed-exposure study used retrospective data from 36 team-seasons of 16 elite European soccer teams (627 players, 96 match hamstring injuries). Its observational design precludes causal conclusions, and the authors state that exposures above 95% at two days out may help mitigate match hamstring injuries in elite football.

evidence.excerpt: Retrospective data from 36 team-seasons (16 elite teams performing in top European leagues) were analyzed (627 players, 96 non-contact time loss match hamstring injuries).

While the present observational study design precludes the examination of causal relationships, the programming of > 95% MSS exposures at D-2 may help mitigate match hamstring injury occurrences in elite football.

claims.text: In an elite football study of expert views on return to play, a main theme was that, when subsequent injury risk is the criterion, players generally return too early.

evidence.excerpt: When the risk of a subsequent injury is taken as the criterion, players generally return to early.

claims.text: The experts' suspected mechanisms for lower risk with longer rehabilitation included incomplete tissue maturation and more time for athletic and football-specific conditioning and psychological readiness.

evidence.excerpt: The suspected mechanisms included incomplete tissue maturation (“Ligamentation takes two years.”) as well as more time for (athletic and football specific) conditioning and ensuring psychological readiness.

claims.text: In elite Australian football players, the authors suggest that prematch perceived wellness does not relate to external match load.

evidence.excerpt: The results of this study suggest that prematch perceived wellness does not relate to external match load in elite Australian football players.

assumptions: A 72 to 96 hour window is treated as roughly a three- to four-day turnaround in the sense used by the speed-exposure study.
High-minute means most of the last competition, low-minute means little or no competition time, and returning means athletes still on a medical or rehabilitation plan.
Sex and specific sport were not given, so transferability is judged for a mixed or unspecified collegiate team sport roster.
coverageGaps: No evidence on strength or weight-room exposure for high-minute, low-minute, or returning athletes during short turnarounds.
No study tests a compensatory running or conditioning top-up dose for low-minute athletes, or shows that top-ups improve readiness or reduce injury.
No collegiate, female, or non-football team sport data on subgroup exposure between competitions.
No data on how returning athletes should be integrated into a full-team session during a 72 to 96 hour turnaround.
